## What does model validation mean?

Validation of an insurance pricing model is broader than comparing fit
statistics. A model may describe the estimation data well while producing
unstable, weakly supported or actuarially implausible tariff relativities.
Conversely, a statistically detectable imperfection may have little practical
pricing effect in the insured portfolio.

No single metric determines whether a model is adequate. A validation review
normally combines several dimensions:

| Dimension | Practical question |
|---|---|
| Statistical adequacy | Are the model structure and distribution broadly consistent with the data? |
| Predictive performance | How well does the model predict the relevant outcome, preferably outside the estimation sample where appropriate? |
| Stability | How sensitive are estimates or performance to variation in the observed sample? |
| Tariff plausibility | Are the effects interpretable, credible and suitable for the intended tariff? |
| Portfolio behaviour | Where does expected experience differ systematically from observed experience? |

These dimensions are complementary rather than a mandatory sequence. Their
relative importance depends on the response, portfolio, modelling objective
and intended use of the tariff.

This vignette starts from fitted models. [Getting Started](getting-started.html)
provides the worked modelling example, while
[Pricing workflow and package building blocks](pricing-workflow-building-blocks.html)
maps validation within the wider package.

## Validation map

The following functions support different validation questions. Not every
model requires every diagnostic.

| Validation question | Typical tool |
|---|---|
| How do alternative fitted models compare? | `model_performance()` |
| Are tariff relativities plausible and sufficiently supported? | `rating_table()` |
| Does marginal observed experience support the fitted pattern? | `add_factor_experience()` |
| How sensitive is measured performance to portfolio resampling? | `validate_performance()` |
| How sensitive are the fitted coefficients to portfolio resampling? | `coefficient_stability()` |
| Is a Poisson frequency model materially overdispersed? | `check_overdispersion()` |
| Do simulation-based residuals show remaining structure? | `check_residuals()` |
| Where does the model over- or under-predict? | `calibration_analysis()` |

## Compact example setup

Most examples use two Poisson frequency models fitted to the same records,
response and exposure definition. Each prediction is an expected claim count
for the observed policy period because it includes the earned-exposure offset.

```{r, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(insurancerating)

portfolio <- as.data.frame(MTPL2)
portfolio$area <- factor(portfolio$area)
portfolio$area <- set_reference_level(portfolio$area, portfolio$exposure)

intercept_model <- glm(
  nclaims ~ 1 + offset(log(exposure)),
  family = poisson(),
  data = portfolio
)

area_model <- glm(
  nclaims ~ area + offset(log(exposure)),
  family = poisson(),
  data = portfolio
)
```

The fitted model is starting material here; construction of frequency,
severity and technical risk-premium models is covered elsewhere.

## Comparing model performance

```{r}
model_performance(intercept_model, area_model)
```

`model_performance()` reports AIC, BIC, response-scale RMSE and residual deviance:

- AIC and BIC compare likelihood fit while penalising model complexity;
- residual deviance describes the remaining lack of fit on the estimation data;
- RMSE summarises prediction error in the response unit and gives relatively
  high weight to large errors because it squares them. The RMSE itself is
  unweighted. Here the response unit is claim count, not claims per unit exposure.

These values are most directly comparable when models use the same response,
estimation records, weights and offsets, as they do here. Residual deviances
should also be compared within the same model family. RMSE uses only the rows
retained in the fit. None of these values establishes
performance on a future portfolio.

Lower values can support a model comparison, but a small improvement does not
automatically imply a better tariff. Exposure by level, coefficient stability,
residual behaviour, observed experience and practical interpretability remain
part of the assessment.

## Inspecting tariff structure and observed experience

`rating_table()` expresses fitted GLM effects as tariff relativities and shows
the exposure supporting each level. This makes the statistical output easier
to review in actuarial terms. Observed experience can be attached to the same
table for a direct graphical comparison.

For this comparison, use `MTPL`, which also contains policyholder age.
The model estimates regional effects at the same age, while the observed
frequency reflects each region's actual mix of ages.

```{r, fig.alt = "Modelled regional relativities adjusted for age and observed claim-frequency relativities, with exposure by region."}
tariff_portfolio <- as.data.frame(MTPL)
tariff_portfolio$zip <- set_reference_level(
  factor(tariff_portfolio$zip), tariff_portfolio$exposure
)

tariff_model <- glm(
  nclaims ~ zip + age_policyholder + offset(log(exposure)),
  family = poisson(), data = tariff_portfolio
)

tariff_table <- rating_table(
  "Age-adjusted model" = tariff_model,
  model_data = tariff_portfolio,
  exposure = "exposure"
)

tariff_table

tariff_review <- tariff_table |>
  add_factor_experience(
    data = tariff_portfolio,
    risk_factors = "zip",
    claim_count = "nclaims",
    exposure = "exposure",
    metric = "frequency",
    label = "Observed frequency"
  )

autoplot(
  tariff_review,
  risk_factors = "zip",
  metric = "frequency"
)
```

A model with slightly better aggregate fit can still be unattractive when it
creates volatile neighbouring relativities, extreme effects supported by
little exposure or shapes without a plausible risk interpretation. An extreme
coefficient in a small segment should therefore not be interpreted in the same
way as the same coefficient supported by a substantial share of the portfolio.

For region 0, the observed frequency is about 2.5% below the reference
region's frequency, while the fitted model estimates almost no difference
at the same age. Region 0 also has relatively little exposure. The gap
is a reason to look at the age mix and claim volume, not evidence by itself
of poor calibration. Use `calibration_analysis()` to compare full-model
predictions with actual outcomes.

## Assessing resampling stability

Unlike `model_performance()`, `validate_performance()` refits the model for
each sample. By default, it fits and scores on the same bootstrap sample.
The example below instead scores on rows left out of each fit.

```{r}
set.seed(123)

resample_result <- validate_performance(
  area_model,
  portfolio,
  n_resamples = 50,
  sample_fraction = 0.8,
  sampling = "bootstrap",
  show_progress = FALSE,
  metrics = c("rmse", "mae", "deviance")
)

head(resample_result$scores)
autoplot(resample_result, metric = "rmse")
```

Here, `sample_fraction = 0.8` means 80 draws per 100 rows, **with replacement**.
Some rows can be drawn more than once. The model is scored on rows not
used for training (the *out-of-bag* rows), not on a fixed 20% test set.
With `sampling = "split"` and a fraction below 1, the draw is without
replacement and the remaining rows are held out.

RMSE and MAE measure error in claim counts here. The dashed orange line is
the original model's RMSE on the full supplied portfolio, not on the
out-of-bag rows used for the histogram. The table also reports predictive
deviance: the same calculation as residual deviance, applied to the evaluation
rows and their predictions. Total deviance depends on the number and weight
of those rows as well as prediction quality.

A wide spread of scores may reflect differences between refitted models,
differences in the claim mix of the evaluation samples, or both. Use
`coefficient_stability()` to examine the fitted effects themselves.
Evaluation on out-of-bag or split rows is out of sample for each refit, but
does not replace validation on a later or external portfolio.

### How stable are the tariff relativities?

`coefficient_stability()` draws rows with replacement from the estimation
portfolio and refits the GLM. It summarises the fitted effects, not
prediction errors. For this log-link model, `scale = "relativity"` expresses
each area effect as a ratio to the original reference area.

```{r}
area_stability <- coefficient_stability(
  area_model, n_resamples = 100, seed = 123, show_progress = FALSE
)
effects <- summary(area_stability, scale = "relativity")
knitr::kable(
  effects[effects$term != "(Intercept)",
          c("term", "estimate", "lower", "upper", "n_successful", "n_requested")],
  digits = 2
)
```

Read the interval together with `n_successful`, the number of comparable
estimates for that effect. A refit can converge without yielding a
comparable estimate for every level, for example when a reference level
is absent from the draw. A narrow interval based on few usable draws
offers little reassurance. Area 0 has about 13 policy-years and one claim
in the estimation portfolio, so interpret its interval with that limited
experience in mind.

## Testing on later periods

Rolling validation fits the specification on earlier periods and scores it
on the next period or periods. The training window expands one period at a
time. The example years here illustrate the interface; MTPL2 has no actual
calendar-year information.

```{r}
temporal_data <- as.data.frame(MTPL2)
temporal_data$year <- rep(2020:2025, length.out = nrow(temporal_data))
temporal_model <- glm(
  nclaims ~ factor(area) + offset(log(exposure)),
  family = poisson(), data = temporal_data
)
validate_performance(
  temporal_model, temporal_data, sampling = "rolling", time = "year",
  initial = 3, metrics = c("rmse", "mae", "deviance"), show_progress = FALSE
)
```

Use actual historical periods to assess temporal predictive performance.
Unlike plotting calibration by year for a fixed model, this refits the model
on only the information available in each training window.

## Checking distributional assumptions

### Overdispersion

```{r}
dispersion_check <- check_overdispersion(area_model)
dispersion_check
```

For a Poisson frequency GLM, the dispersion ratio is Pearson's chi-squared
statistic divided by the residual degrees of freedom. A value above one means
that observed variation exceeds the variance implied by the Poisson model.

Both statistical evidence and practical magnitude matter. In a large insurance
portfolio, a small departure can produce a very small p-value simply because
many observations are available. The size of the dispersion ratio and its
effect on uncertainty and tariff decisions are generally more informative than
the p-value alone. Overdispersion can indicate omitted heterogeneity,
clustering, unusual observations or model misspecification, but does not by
itself identify the cause.

### Simulation-based residuals

```{r, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
set.seed(123)

residual_check <- check_residuals(
  area_model,
  n_simulations = 250
)

autoplot(residual_check)
```

`check_residuals()` uses DHARMa simulations from the fitted model to construct
scaled residuals. The QQ plot and uniformity test assess whether the observed
response behaves consistently with the distribution implied by that model.

Systematic departures can indicate remaining structure, distributional
mismatch or unusual observations. The uniformity p-value is a diagnostic signal,
not a stand-alone acceptance rule. Its interpretation should be combined with
the location and shape of departures, fitted values, exposure and relevant
risk-factor levels.

## Reviewing observed versus expected experience

Use `calibration_analysis()` to compare observed and expected outcomes overall
and within segments. Here the predictions include earned exposure, so
both totals are claim counts.

```{r}
calibration_analysis(area_model, portfolio)
area_calibration <- calibration_analysis(area_model, portfolio, by = "area")
area_calibration
autoplot(area_calibration)
```

O/E is observed claims divided by expected claims. A ratio above 1 means more
claims were observed than expected; a ratio below 1 means fewer. The overall
ratio describes calibration-in-the-large.

Here, O/E is 1 in every area: the Poisson model estimates a separate rate for
each area and is evaluated on the same records used to fit it. This illustrates
how to read the output, but does not demonstrate calibration on new data.

Use `by = "year"` when the evaluation data contain a calendar year. A change
in O/E across years can indicate a change in the overall prediction level,
even if the model still ranks high- and low-risk policies equally well.
`autoplot()` shows that comparison as an O/E line over time.
To check whether the pattern differs by area, use `by = c("year", "area")`.
This gives one row per observed year and area combination, with their
exposure and claim totals. The plot shows a point per combination rather
than joining areas into a single time series.

### Does the model get claim frequency right at different risk levels?

With `groups = 5`, the function sorts policy records from lowest to highest
**predicted claims per policy-year**. Dividing each prediction by its exposure
for this ranking means a longer policy period is not treated as a higher
risk just because more claims are expected during it.

The sorted records are split into five groups. Group 1 contains the lowest
predicted risks and group 5 the highest. Each group aims for about 20% of
the portfolio's total exposure, not 20% of the policies. These are groups
of model predictions, not rating-factor levels such as area. Policies with
the same predicted frequency can fall on either side of a group boundary;
ties follow the input row order.

```{r, fig.alt = "Observed against expected claims per policy-year for five groups of predicted risk, with a diagonal line where the frequencies are equal."}
risk_calibration <- calibration_analysis(area_model, portfolio, groups = 5)
knitr::kable(risk_calibration, digits = 2)
autoplot(risk_calibration)
```

Each dot is one group. Its x-coordinate is total expected claims divided
by the group's total policy-years; its y-coordinate is total observed claims
divided by the same policy-years. For group 2 (the second dot from the left),
there were
`r risk_calibration$Observed[2]` observed claims versus about
`r round(risk_calibration$Expected[2])` expected, so the dot lies **above**
the diagonal: the model predicted too few claims for that group. A dot
below the diagonal means it predicted too many.

This is a visual check for systematic over- or under-prediction, not a
statistical test or a measure of how well the model ranks individual risks.
Read a gap alongside the group's exposure and claim volume: a large O/E
deviation based on few claims may have little credibility. This example uses
the estimation data; use separate evaluation data to assess calibration on
unseen policies. For model-point aggregation before modelling rather than
calibration, see [Large Portfolios](large-portfolios.html).

## Validation, investigation and refinement

### Comparing expected claims before and after refinement

For a model returned by `refit()`, the original portfolio may not contain
the columns added by smoothing or restrictions. To check the refit's own
portfolio, use `extract_model_data(refined_model)`. For a smoothed model,
group by the column containing the new tariff bands (for example,
`by = "age_smooth"` if the source variable was `age`), rather than by the
numeric relativity column used in the offset. On separate evaluation data,
apply the same refinement mappings to those rows first.

To check a restriction, put **observed claims, expected claims before and
expected claims after** side by side. Use the same records and the same
grouping column for both models so that any change comes from the predictions
rather than a change in portfolio mix.

```{r}
restricted_model <- prepare_refinement(area_model, data = portfolio) |>
  add_restriction(c("3" = 1.10), model_variable = "area") |>
  refit()

evaluation <- extract_model_data(restricted_model)
before <- calibration_analysis(area_model, evaluation, by = "area")
after <- calibration_analysis(restricted_model, evaluation, by = "area")

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Area = after$area,
  Exposure = after$Exposure,
  Observed = after$Observed,
  Expected_before = before$Expected,
  Expected_after = after$Expected
), digits = 2)
```

Use fixed bands or rating-factor levels for this comparison. With
`groups = 5`, each model can rank policies differently, so its group 1
need not contain the same policies as group 1 from the other model.

### Acting on validation findings

Validation identifies evidence; it should not silently alter the model. A
useful response to an issue is:

1. identify the affected observations or tariff levels;
2. investigate the likely cause;
3. revise the data or model when the statistical specification is responsible;
4. apply an explicit actuarial refinement only when it has a defensible tariff
   rationale;
5. validate the resulting model again.

Incorrect exposure, data-quality problems, missing interactions, poor
segmentation, inappropriate distributions and large-loss treatment can all
produce unattractive diagnostics. These issues may require revisiting the model
rather than smoothing or restricting its coefficients. The
[Refinement building blocks](refinement-workflow.html) vignette explains how
justified tariff adjustments can be recorded and refitted explicitly.

## Putting the evidence together

Validation should combine evidence rather than rank models on one metric. A
model may have a slightly lower AIC but unstable coefficients, weak observed
support and material residual structure. Such a model may be less suitable for
tariff implementation than a more stable alternative.

Conversely, a statistically significant diagnostic result may have little
practical effect when its magnitude is small and portfolio behaviour remains
stable. The conclusion should reflect statistical adequacy, predictive
evidence, sampling stability, exposure and credibility, actuarial plausibility
and the intended pricing use.
